© Bootcamp.com 4 slatnemadnuF 4. Alterations to Perfusion & Interventions Perfusion is affected by problems with the heart (contractility), the vessels (preload/afterload), or the blood itself. The goal in caring for a client with impaired perfusion is to restore circulation, which helps protect organs and prevent complications. For clients with impaired perfusion: y Monitor vital signs and perfusion status continuously (see TABLE 2).  Provide oxygen (nasal cannula) to maintain oxygen saturation >90%. y Address underlying conditions (e.g., heart failure, blood clots, shock) to restore effective circulation (TABLE 5).  Encourage lifestyle changes to prevent atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, the leading cause of death and contributor to stroke, heart attack, and peripheral vascular disease. y Teach clients about smoking cessation and to reduce alcohol intake. y Engage in exercise to maintain normal body weight. y Eat a heart-healthy diet (fruits, vegetables, low-fat dairy products, low saturated fats, and low-sodium). Oxygen Delivery Oxygenation © Bootcamp.com 8 yrotaripseR 1. O xygenation Oxygenation refers to how well FIGURE 1. OXYGENATION oxygen (O ) is delivered to the 2 tissues of the body (FIGURE 1). Oxygenation occurs through: 1. Ventilation: When we breathe in, air enters the lungs, bringing oxygen into the alveoli (tiny air sacs in the lungs). 2. Gas exchange: Oxygen  diffuses from the alveoli Pulmonary capillaries, where it binds to hemoglobin in red blood cells. 3. Transport: The heart pumps oxygen-rich blood through the body to deliver oxygen to the tissues. Adequate oxygenation is essential for organ function. Impaired oxygenation can cause these life-threatening complications: y Hypoxemia:  oxygen in the blood y Hypoxia:  oxygen in tissues Signs of hypoxia  Early: Restlessness, confusion, tachycardia, tachypnea, accessory muscle use, and tripod position (sitting upright, leaning forward on hands) y Late: Cyanosis, bradypnea, and bradycardia  Recognizing hypoxia: Restlessness and tachypnea are early signs of hypoxia. Late signs are cyanosis, bradycardia, and bradypnea.
